correctness.rationale: The proof reduces every possible four-deficient-divisor choice to one of exactly fifteen explicit factorizations. Positivity of the two factors is justified from \(\Delta>0\), \(p<q\), and the coefficient bounds. Exhausting all divisors of \(K_E\le39\) leaves exactly three prime pairs, and direct substitution verifies all three witnesses. The included verifier independently regenerates the complete certificate.

originality.rationale: The closest published-result match classifies the exactly \(3\)-deficient-perfect squarefree \(2pq\) case, not the four-deficient-divisor equation. Chen 2019 classifies odd exactly \(2\)-deficient-perfect numbers with two prime factors, and Aursukaree--Pongsriiam 2020/2021 classifies odd exactly \(3\)-deficient-perfect numbers with at most two prime factors. OEIS A331627 is a membership table for some \(k\) and does not state or prove the exact \(k=4\), squarefree-three-prime classification. The searched sources therefore do not imply the new theorem.
residual_risks: The terminology is specialized, so an uncatalogued thesis or non-indexed note could conceivably contain the same finite classification; no such source was found in the checked primary literature, database, web, or published-result searches.

value.rationale: Exactly \(k\)-deficient-perfect numbers are an established family studied for \(k=2\) and \(k=3\). The even squarefree three-prime support \(2pq\) is a natural first three-prime support beyond the previously emphasized two-prime classifications, and \(k=4\) is the next natural exact-deficiency layer. A complete bound-free classification on this slice therefore resolves a motivated structural boundary rather than an arbitrary finite search.
